questions.q: The WHO haemoglobin threshold for anaemia in an average healthy 40-year-old male is:
questions.exp: The p66 definition gives male Hb <13 g/dL. (Book p66)

questions.q: The female haemoglobin threshold shown beside the healthy-adult definition is:
questions.exp: The page gives female Hb <12 g/dL. (Book p66)

questions.q: The haemoglobin threshold printed for a pregnant woman is:
questions.exp: The pregnancy threshold is <11 g/dL. (Book p66)

questions.q: The p66 definition lists which haemoglobin threshold for a patient with CKD?
questions.exp: The page lists Hb <10 g/dL for a known CKD patient. (Book p66)

questions.q: The top cell in the haematopoiesis diagram is the:
questions.exp: The diagram begins with pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (PPHSC). (Book p66)

questions.q: The two progenitor branches directly downstream of PPHSC are:
opts: Common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors
questions.exp: PPHSC branches to common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors. (Book p66)

questions.q: Which set is shown downstream of the common myeloid progenitor?
opts: B/T lymphocytes and NK cells only
Eosinophils, B cells and platelets only
questions.exp: The common myeloid progenitor gives platelets, granulocytes, monocytes and RBCs. (Book p66)

questions.q: The common lymphoid progenitor branch gives rise to:
questions.exp: The diagram shows B/T lymphocytes and NK cells downstream of the common lymphoid progenitor. (Book p66)

questions.q: Which trio is included under granulocytes in the p66 lineage diagram?
opts: B cells, T cells and plasma cells
questions.exp: The listed granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. (Book p66)

questions.q: The monocyte branch is shown giving rise to:
questions.exp: Monocytes are shown differentiating into macrophages. (Book p66)

questions.q: Which sequence gives the early red-cell production pathway in the figure?
opts: PPHSC → common lymphoid progenitor → NK cell → CFU-E → RBC
PPHSC → common myeloid progenitor → BFU-E → CFU-E → proerythroblast → mature RBC
questions.exp: The figure traces PPHSC through CMP, BFU-E, CFU-E and proerythroblast to mature RBCs. (Book p66)

questions.q: The stage labelled EPO-independent and iron-independent is:
questions.exp: The diagram marks the common myeloid progenitor as EPO-independent and iron-independent. (Book p66)

questions.q: The BFU-E stage is labelled:
questions.exp: BFU-E is marked EPO-dependent, iron-independent. (Book p66)

questions.q: The p66 bracket labels the CFU-E stage and downstream red-cell maturation as dependent on:
questions.exp: The bracket begins at CFU-E and continues through mature RBCs; it labels dependence on both EPO and iron. (Book p66)

questions.q: Erythropoietin is produced by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the:
opts: Cortex and outer medulla of the kidney
questions.exp: The note locates EPO production in peritubular interstitial fibroblasts of the renal cortex and outer medulla. (Book p66)

questions.q: The source named for thrombopoietin is the:
questions.exp: The note says thrombopoietin is produced by the liver for platelets. (Book p66)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — as erythroid cells mature, the page shows cell size and number of nucleoli decreasing.
opts: False — cell size decreases but nucleoli increase
questions.exp: The p66 note says nucleoli decrease with chromatin condensation and cell size also decreases as maturity increases. (Book p66)

questions.q: The pro-normoblast/pro-erythroblast is described as the:
questions.exp: The page labels the pro-normoblast as the largest cell. (Book p67)

questions.q: Which cytoplasmic colour is listed for the pro-normoblast?
questions.exp: The pro-normoblast cytoplasm is basophilic. (Book p67)

questions.q: The pro-normoblast has nucleoli because the chromatin is:
questions.exp: Nucleoli are present due to fine chromatin in the pro-normoblast. (Book p67)

questions.q: The pro-normoblast nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio is:
opts: Absent because the nucleus has been lost
questions.exp: A high N:C ratio is listed for the pro-normoblast. (Book p67)

questions.q: Which pair describes the early/basophilic normoblast?
opts: Basophilic cytoplasm; nucleoli absent as chromatin condensation begins
No nucleus; bluish tinge from RNA
questions.exp: The early normoblast remains basophilic; nucleoli are absent as chromatin condensation begins. (Book p67)

questions.q: The nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio remains high in which early precursor after the pro-normoblast?
questions.exp: The early/basophilic normoblast is also described with a high N:C ratio. (Book p67)

questions.q: The intermediate/polychromatic normoblast has grayish cytoplasm because of:
questions.exp: The gray colour is attributed to the beginning of haemoglobin synthesis. (Book p67)

questions.q: The nucleus of the intermediate/polychromatic normoblast is described as:
opts: Dense and pyknotic with red cytoplasm
questions.exp: The page describes a rounded nucleus and positive chromatin condensation/clumping. (Book p67)

questions.q: At which erythroid stage does cell division cease according to p67?
questions.exp: Cell division is stated to cease at the intermediate/polychromatic stage. (Book p67)

questions.q: The late/orthochromatic normoblast cytoplasm is reddish because it is:
questions.exp: The reddish cytoplasm is attributed to being well haemoglobinised. (Book p67)

questions.q: The nucleus of the late/orthochromatic normoblast is:
questions.exp: The late normoblast has a dense, pyknotic nucleus. (Book p67)

questions.q: Which pair characterizes a reticulocyte in the stage diagram?
opts: Nucleus absent; cytoplasm has a bluish tinge from RNA
questions.exp: The reticulocyte has no nucleus and a bluish cytoplasmic tinge due to RNA. (Book p67)

questions.q: The mature RBC image is described as being shown after:
questions.exp: The image caption says mature RBCs after Romanowsky staining. (Book p67)

questions.q: A giant pro-erythroblast is noted in:
questions.exp: The p67 note associates a giant pro-erythroblast with pure red cell aplasia. (Book p67)

questions.q: Reticulocyte RNA is detected using which class of stain?
questions.exp: The page says reticulocyte RNA requires supravital staining. (Book p68)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — fixation is required before supravital staining to detect reticulocyte RNA.
opts: True — fixation is required for every reticulocyte test
False — but only for Romanowsky stain
questions.exp: The page explicitly notes fixation is not required for detecting RNA with supravital stain. (Book p68)

questions.q: Which pair of supravital stains is listed for reticulocytes?
opts: Brilliant cresyl blue and new methylene blue
questions.exp: The listed stains are brilliant cresyl blue and new methylene blue. (Book p68)

questions.q: With Romanowsky stain, reticulocytes are noted to appear:
opts: Polychromatic; the reticulocyte RNA is not detected
questions.exp: The note says RNA is not detected with Romanowsky stain and cells appear polychromatic. (Book p68)

questions.q: The normal reticulocyte count range printed on p68 is:
questions.exp: The page gives a normal RC of 0.5–1.5%. (Book p68)

questions.q: In hypoproliferative anaemia, reduced RBC production leads to:
questions.exp: Reduced RBC production is linked to reticulocytopenia/decreased reticulocyte count. (Book p68)

questions.q: A hyperproliferative response associated with RBC destruction or blood loss produces:
opts: A normal count in every case
questions.exp: Increased destruction or blood loss is linked to reticulocytosis. (Book p68)

questions.q: The absolute reticulocyte count range shown is:
questions.exp: The page gives an absolute count of 25,000–75,000 cells/µL. (Book p68)

questions.q: The corrected reticulocyte count (CRC) corrects for:
questions.exp: CRC is described as correction for the degree of anaemia. (Book p68)

questions.q: Which equation reproduces the corrected reticulocyte count formula?
opts: Patient haemoglobin × desired haemoglobin ÷ reticulocyte count
questions.exp: CRC = reticulocyte count × haemoglobin in patient / desired haemoglobin level. (Book p68)

questions.q: The desired haemoglobin value used for a male in the CRC note is:
questions.exp: The boxed desired Hb value is 15 g/dL for males. (Book p68)

questions.q: The desired haemoglobin value used for a female in the CRC note is:
questions.exp: The boxed desired Hb value is 13 g/dL for females. (Book p68)

questions.q: The reticulocyte production index (RPI) additionally corrects for:
opts: The shorter lifespan of mature RBCs only
The longer life of prematurely released reticulocytes
questions.exp: RPI corrects for the longer life of prematurely released reticulocytes. (Book p68)

questions.q: The p68 formula for RPI is:
opts: Hb divided by absolute reticulocyte count
questions.exp: The page gives RPI = CRC/2. (Book p68)

questions.q: A male with Hb 9 g/dL has a reticulocyte count of 6%. Using the desired male Hb and CRC formula on p68, what is his corrected reticulocyte count?
questions.exp: CRC = 6% × (9/15) = 3.6%; 1.8% would be the page's subsequent RPI calculation after dividing CRC by 2. (Book p68)

questions.q: The first branch in the clinical-approach flowchart separates anaemia by:
questions.exp: The first decision is single-lineage versus multiple-lineage involvement. (Book p69)

questions.q: In the p69 flowchart, RPI below what threshold is labelled hypoproliferative anaemia?
questions.exp: RPI <2.5 is labelled hypoproliferative. (Book p69)

questions.q: An RPI above what threshold is labelled hyperproliferative anaemia?
questions.exp: RPI >2.5 is labelled hyperproliferative. (Book p69)

questions.q: The normocytic MCV interval written in the flowchart is:
questions.exp: The note defines average RBC MCV as 80–100 fL. (Book p69)

questions.q: The microcytic branch uses which MCV cutoff?
questions.exp: The flowchart places microcytosis below 80 fL. (Book p69)

questions.q: The macrocytic branch uses which MCV cutoff?
questions.exp: The flowchart defines macrocytosis as >100 fL. (Book p69)

questions.q: Which group appears under the normocytic/microcytic hypoproliferative branch?
opts: Iron-deficiency anaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia and thalassaemia trait
Aplastic anaemia and pure red-cell aplasia only
Autoimmune haemolysis, G6PD deficiency and malaria
questions.exp: The flowchart lists iron deficiency, chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia and thalassaemia trait under normo/microcytic disease. (Book p69)

questions.q: The macrocytic branch in the flowchart points to:
opts: Iron-deficiency anaemia due to blood loss
Megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency
Sideroblastic anaemia due to alcohol only
questions.exp: The macrocytic branch is labelled megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency. (Book p69)

questions.q: Megaloblasts are described as RBC precursors with delayed:
opts: Nuclear maturation despite normal cytoplasmic maturation
Haemoglobin synthesis with normal cell division
questions.exp: The note defines megaloblasts as RBCs lagging in nuclear maturation with normal cytoplasmic maturation. (Book p69)

questions.q: The page estimates marrow cellularity as:
questions.exp: The note gives marrow cellularity = 100 − age of the person. (Book p69)

questions.q: For a 50-year-old person, the marrow-cellularity example predicts approximately:
questions.exp: The example says a 50-year-old has 50% fat and 50% cellular marrow. (Book p69)

questions.q: The marrow-failure example says all cells are replaced by fat, as in:
questions.exp: The note names aplastic anaemia as an example of marrow failure with replacement by fat. (Book p69)

questions.q: The normal myeloid-to-erythroid (M:E) ratio listed is:
questions.exp: The page gives a normal M:E ratio of 3:1. (Book p69)

questions.q: Which marrow image is captioned separately from the two hyperplasia examples?
questions.exp: The three image captions are normal bone marrow, myeloid hyperplasia and erythroid hyperplasia. (Book p69)

questions.q: The bottom-left marrow image is captioned:
questions.exp: The bottom-left image is labelled myeloid hyperplasia. (Book p69)

questions.q: The bottom-right marrow image is captioned:
questions.exp: The bottom-right image is labelled erythroid hyperplasia. (Book p69)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the flowchart first evaluates lineage involvement, then uses RPI and MCV for a single-lineage anaemia branch.
opts: False — RPI is not used in the flowchart
False — MCV is assessed before lineage
True — but only for multiple-lineage disease
True — lineage → RPI → MCV is the displayed sequence
questions.exp: The diagram begins with single versus multiple lineages; the single-lineage branch then divides by RPI and MCV. (Book p69)

units.title: WHO Thresholds & Haematopoiesis
units.guide:
Hb thresholds on p66: male <13, female <12, pregnancy <11 and CKD <10 g/dL.
PPHSC splits to myeloid and lymphoid progenitors; the chart traces RBC stages.
EPO is renal; thrombopoietin is hepatic; early erythroid stages differ in EPO/iron dependence.

units.title: Erythroid Maturation
units.guide:
Pro-normoblast is largest and nucleolated; early normoblast loses nucleoli.
Polychromatic cells become gray, round-nucleated and stop dividing; orthochromatic cells are red/pyknotic.
Reticulocytes lose the nucleus but retain RNA; a giant proerythroblast is noted in pure red-cell aplasia.

units.title: Reticulocytes and Indices
units.guide:
Supravital dyes detect reticulocyte RNA; normal count 0.5–1.5%, absolute 25,000–75,000/µL.
Low production → reticulocytopenia; destruction/loss → reticulocytosis.
CRC corrects for anaemia; RPI also corrects for premature-reticulocyte lifespan.

units.title: Approach & Marrow Notes
units.guide:
Start with lineages, then RPI (<2.5 hypo; >2.5 hyper) and MCV (<80, 80–100, >100 fL).
The page lists hypoproliferative causes and marrow images/ratio.
Cellularity = 100 − age; normal M:E = 3:1; marrow failure replaces cells with fat.
